text: Practice Set 1: Solutions Problem 1: The pseudocode for insertion sort was given in class: for i = 2 to n for j = i down to 2 If A [j] < A [j − 1] Swap A [j] and A [j − 1] else break Number of swaps: In the best-case scenario, the array is already sorted. Note that there are 0 swaps performed in this case. In the worst-case scenario, the array is sorted in reverse order. The first iteration of the above loop performs one swap. The second iteration performs two swaps, etc. The last iteration performs n − 1 swaps. Therefore the total number of swaps in the worst-case is 1 + 2 + . . . + (n − 1) = n2 2 − n 2 Number of comparisons: The best-case scenario is when the array is already sorted. At each iteration of the outer for-loop, the inner for-loop only performs one comparison, and then breaks. There are n − 1 executions of the inner for-loop, and so there are a total of n − 1 comparisons. The worst-case scenario was examined in class, and we showed that the worst-case number of comparisons is n 2 2 − n 2 Problem 2: The outer for loop of insertion sort carries out n−1 iterations. If the array is already sorted, the inner for loop will perform a single comparison, and then break. Therefore each iteration of the inner for loop runs in constant time, c. Any initial operations performed by the function also run in constant time, d. Therefore the total best-case runtime is T (n) = c(n−1)+d. We can show that this is O(n) because T (n) = cn − c + d ≤ (c + d)n. In summary, the best-case runtime of Insertion sort is O(n) and the worst-case runtime of insertion sort (shown in class) is O(n2). It turns out that on average the runtime of insertion sort is nevertheless O(n2). Problem 3: The reverse procedure will swap elements at opposite ends of the array. The for loop proceeds through half the array making swaps. Note that the index of the lower median is ⌊(j + i)/2⌋. Therefore the swapping can terminate at index ⌊(j + i)/2⌋. Reverse(A, i, j) ind = j for k = i to ⌊(j + i)/2⌋ Swap A [k] and A[ ind ] ind = ind - 1 If array A contains n elements, the algorithm carries out a for loop of exactly ⌊n/2⌋ iterations, regardless of the input ordering. Therefore the best and worst-case runtimes are the same. Each iteration of the for loop runs in constant time. Therefore the runtime of algorithm is T (n) = a n 2 + b for some constant a. This can be shown to be O(n) as follows: T (n) = a · n 2 + b ≤ (a + b)n for all n ≥ 1. By definition of big-oh, the reverse algorithm runs in time O(n). Problem 4 Selection sort works by continuously selecting the minimum from the unsorted section of the array, and then placing it in the sorted section of the array, using a swap. Suppose the input to the algorithm is array A indexed from 1 to n. The pseudo-code is given below: for i= 1 to n-1 min_index = i for j = i+1 to n if A[j] < A[min_index] min_index = j Swap A[min_index] and A[i] 1 Each iteration of the the inner for loop runs in constant time, say d. There are n − 1 iterations of the inner for-loop when i = 1, accounting for a total time of d(n − 1). There are n − 2 iterations of the inner for-loop when i = 2, accounting for a total time of d(n − 2). The pattern continues and the sum of all the operations carried out by the inner for loop is exactly: d(n − 1) + d(n − 2) + . . . + d(1) = d ( n(n − 1) 2 ) There are also exactly n − 1 swaps that are performed, and each swap takes constant time, say k, accounting for k(n − 1) time. The total runtime is therefore d ( n(n−1) 2 ) + k(n − 1). We can show this is O(n2): T (n) = d ( n(n − 1) 2 ) + k(n − 1) ≤ dn 2/2 + kn ≤ dn 2 + kn 2 = (d + k)n2 Note that in the above analysis, the number of steps performed is always the same, regardless of the input. Therefore the best-case and worst-case runtimes are identical: they are both O(n2). This differs from Insertion Sort, which has a best-case runtime of O(n). Therefore if there is a high chance that your input is sorted, Insertion sort should be preferred. Problem 5: Option 1: constant amount of extra space Use variables max-index and max-count to keep track of the index of the most-common element, and the count of the most-common element. We use brute force to loop through the array counting the number of occurrences of each element. Note that this procedure runs in time Θ(n 2). maxcount = 0 for i = 1 to n count = 0 for j = 1 to n if A[j] = A[i] count++ if count > maxcount maxcount = count maxindex = i Option 2: use extra space, but algorithm is faster We could create an external array (or hashtable) that stores the number of occurrences of each element. For example, if array A contained elements that are numbers from 1 to m, then we could create an external table T [1, 2, . . . , m]. Then we simply loop through A, and for every element k that we encounter, we increment T [k]. In this way, T [k] stores the number of occurrences of element k. Initialise T [1, . . . , m] = 0 for i = 1 to n T[A[i]] ++ Now we can finish by simply looping through T and finding the maximum. Problem 6 Assume that the input to Bubble sort is an array A indexed from 1 to n. The algorithm below passes through the elements of the array and swaps any two adjacent elements that are not in relative order. The process continues until a full pass can be made without any swaps. Bubble-Sort(A [1, . . . , n]) made-swap = true while(made-swap) made-swap = false for i = 1 to n-1 if A[i+1] < A[i] Swap A[i] and A[i+1] made-swap = true Worst-case: If the array is sorted in reverse order, then after each pass of Bubblesort the maximum element of the unsorted section is moved into the last position. For example, starting with 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 after one pass of bubble-sort the array becomes: 4, 3, 2, 1, 5, and after the second pass the array becomes 3, 2, 1, 4, 5. Each pass places exactly one element in its final sorted position, and therefore n passes are required to finish sorting the array. Each pass performs exactly n − 1 2 comparisons in the for-loop, and therefore the worst-case number of comparisons is n(n − 1). The number of swaps in the worst case is identical: The number of swaps made during the first pass is n − 1, during the second is n − 2, etc. Therefore the total number of swaps is n(n − 1)/2 in the worst case. Since the number of swaps and comparisons in the worst-case is of the form T (n) = an2 +bn+c, the run-time is quadratic and is therefore O(n2). Best-case: Bubblesort is effective if the input array is already sorted. It is able to detect this right away, and return the sorted array after one pass. This is because on a sorted array, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, Bubblesort performs no swaps on the first pass, and therefore will not repeat a second pass. Therefore the best-case number of swaps is 0 and the best-case number of comparisons is n − 1. The runtime is therefore T (n) = an + b, which we have shown is O(n). Problem 7: As noted in the previous question, after the first pass of bubble sort, the maximum element is placed in the last position. Therefore the next iteration only needs to verify swaps up to the second last element. The update is shown below: for k = n-1 down to 1 made-swap = false for i = 1 to k if A[i+1] < A[i] Swap A[i] and A[i+1] made-swap = true if made-swap = false break The inner for loop is executed exactly k times, for k = n − 1 down to 1. Each iteration of the inner for loop runs in constant time. As shown in the previous problem, the outer for loop is executed the maximal number of times when the input array is sorted in reverse order. Therefore, the total runtime in the worst case is of the form c(1 + 2 + 3 + . . . + (n − 1)) = c(n(n − 1)/2) = c( n2 2 − n 2 ) ≤ cn 2 and so is O(n2). Problem 8: The LIST object in python is implemented as an array of an initial size (typically small). There is an extra variable that keeps track of how many elements are actually in the list. This is because the array may be larger than the actual list. As objects appended to the list object, they are added to the next free spot in the array, and the list size is incremented. However, if there is more free space, a new larger array is allocated. This new array is often double the size of the previous array. This takes time O(n) in order to copy the elements from the old array into the new array. A similar problem occurs when we remove from the list object. The operation list.remove(5) first requires a search through the array in order to determine if there is an element that is equal to 5. Next, the object 5 is freed (in terms of memory, but all the elements in the array that are after the position 5 must be shifted up. This also takes time O(n). Problem 9: ‹ TRUE.
